Oneg Shabbat

Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Re'eh
a) "The blessing, if ye hearken... and the curse, if ye will not hearken... but turn aside" (11:27–28)
With good, "a good thought — the Holy One, blessed be He, joins it to the deed"; therefore, even when "if ye hearken" — when you merely listen, when there is a good thought — already "the Holy One joins it to the deed", already — the blessing. With evil, on the other hand, one is not punished until one actually does the evil, when one reaches "and turn aside". For merely listening to evil one is not punished... Sfat Emet.
b) "To put His name there" (12:5)
What do the words "to put His name there" mean? Because only in the Temple was it permitted to pronounce God's full name as it is written, and that is the meaning of "to put His name there"... Pnei Yafot.
c) "And ye shall rejoice... and the Levite that is within your gates, for he hath no portion nor inheritance with you" (ibid., 12)
At the time when Jews rejoice over the gathered harvest, the Levite should rejoice precisely because "he hath no portion nor inheritance with you" — because he does not have all the worries, because he need not go through the hard earthly life, because he devotes himself solely to divine service... The Dubno Maggid.
d) "Only be steadfast in not eating the blood" (ibid., 23)
It appears that a time will come when, in order not to eat blood, carrion and non-kosher meat, one will have to wage a hard struggle for it... Leket Amarim.
e) "And this is the manner of the release" (15:2)
The Vilna Gaon was once asked: what is the punishment in the world to come of "one who borrows and does not repay", of a bankrupt? The Torah is strict about robbery even of less than a perutah's worth, and for robbery neither Yom Kippur nor the day of death atones — so what about all those Jews who sometimes go bankrupt out of hardship?
He answered:
In Avot it is told that Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai bade his disciples choose a good way to which a person should hold. Rabbi Eliezer said a good eye, Rabbi Shimon said "one who foresees the outcome", etc.; and when he asked them about the evil way, all said the opposite. Rabbi Eliezer said an evil eye, etc.
Rabbi Shimon, for whom the good way was "one who foresees the outcome", answered "one who borrows and does not repay". One may ask: how is that the opposite of "one who foresees the outcome"?
But Rabbi Shimon means: if the "one who borrows and does not repay" was one who foresaw the outcome, i.e. he knew he would not be able to pay and borrowed nevertheless — he is utterly wicked; but one who did not foresee that a catastrophe would befall him, and misfortune struck him unexpectedly — for him one can plead merit...
f) "Howbeit there shall be no needy among you... if only thou diligently hearken unto the voice of the Lord thy God" (ibid., 5)
If you fulfil God's commandment, if you arrange a state for yourself according to the commandments of the Torah, "if thou diligently hearken unto the voice of the Lord thy God" — then "there shall be no needy among you": it will be altogether impossible for one to be poor and the other rich, exploiters and exploited. Imrei Hen.
g) "And thy heart shall not be grieved when thou givest unto him" (ibid., 10)
After giving, your heart will not ache. You will see: you will have no regret for it...
"The righteous — their beginning is suffering and their end is tranquillity; the wicked — their beginning is tranquillity and their end is suffering." Good is hard at the start and later one is satisfied with it, and with evil it is the reverse. Dvarim Nehmadim.
• • •
Giving support to a poor man we call tzedakah; it comes from the word tzedek, justice, for according to the Jewish conception helping a poor man is not philanthropy but a just deed, since the poor man has a right to our property just as we do. For why [?] should we own more than he, and everything is after all God's [?], what He gave him from God... R. Yosef ibn Kaspi.
h) "And thine eye be evil against thy needy brother... and it be sin in thee" (ibid., 9)
When a poor man comes to ask for alms, the rich man knows how to figure out that he is not pious enough and the like. Thereby he proves that he himself is sinful, for the Gemara says that Jeremiah prayed to God concerning the men of Anathoth that, even when they engage in charity, God should make them stumble with "unworthy poor"; it follows that if the poor man who came his way is not pious enough — "and thine eye be evil against thy needy brother, and it be sin in thee" — he thereby proves that he himself is not [sic; evidently meant: is] sinful, and therefore he is made to stumble with unworthy poor.. R. Sheftel Horowitz.

In the Tangle of Life (6)

[Serialized novel — Kraków, Drohobycz, Hamburg and New York; installment 6.]
(A novel with dramatic events in Kraków, Zawiercie and New York)

He did not get much joy out of the visit. He found his parents much aged and poor — sick, broken people.

In the few days he spent in Kraków he also learned that Malkele was faring very badly: she was very poor and did not live well with her husband. A thought flashed through his head — to say goodbye to Malkele too before he left. He did not think long and went off to Drohobycz.

He knew the address, and that she was now called Berman and had a small spice shop.

And there he went.

At first Malkele did not recognize him. When he had studied in Kraków with her father, he had worn a shtrayml, had sidelocks and went about dressed in a bekeshe; now, however, he went about dressed like a "Deutsch" [i.e. in modern European clothes]. But when he began to speak she recognized him and was very glad to see him.

She told him at once that he had come to her now just like an angel from heaven. She needed him very badly. But here she could not talk with him. In the evening she would meet him on the avenue outside the town.

"Why are you trembling so, Malkele? May one not speak to a person one has known for so long?"

"What are you saying? Have you forgotten already? Drohobycz is a small town; all I need is for someone to see me talking with you — they would drum it all over town at once."

In the evening, on the avenue outside the town, Malkele opened her heart to Dovidl.

"Dear Dovidl, what is one to do? Give me advice. I have fallen into the hands of a fanatical husband, a brute; he beats me, my whole body is covered with bruises."

"But why does he beat you?"

"For nothing. Just this Sabbath I combed my hair a little, and he fell on me like a wild beast. Sometimes he beats me because he doesn't like the food, or because I didn't come into the shop on the minute; over anything at all he sets about[?] beating me — not like a Jew, but like a peasant. I have decided not to stay with him any longer, I can't! I don't have a piece of bread to eat my fill, no decent dress on my body, and on top of that, blows. I will run away wherever my eyes carry me."

"Good, Malkele! You've said exactly the right thing — you will run away with me!"

"Where to?" she looked at him, astonished.

"To America."

"To America?" she cried out in fright. "And my child, my Yosele? No, it's impossible! Besides, my husband has a brother in America!"

"You will go, Malkele, with me — and tomorrow, no less! Leave the child with him for the time being; he will hand him over to you later."

"But will he even know how to handle a child? Why, he'll kill him[?], the murderer!"

"Listen to me, Malkele: I'm going — go with me! I loved you very much and I love you now too; I know that you, too, once loved me very much."

So they talked until late in the evening. When they parted she asked him to come into the shop at about half past seven in the morning, when her husband would be at prayers. But she told him not to count on her going with him to America: she would not leave her child; Yosele was indeed already a child of six, but he needed her.

In the morning, however, when Dovidl came in, he found an entirely different Malkele. Her face was all swollen with bruises[?], her eyes were black and blue, and she could hardly speak.

"Yesterday he beat me like that because I came home late. He literally trampled me with his feet! I'm going with you, Dovid! Take me away from here! Save me!"

"Where shall we meet?"

"Tonight, on the avenue."

In the evening Malkele came with a small bundle and told him that a larger bundle, with a few dresses and linen, she had earlier carried to a peasant woman not far from there[?]. They went there and took the bundle. That very same night they left Drohobycz for Hamburg.

In the few days they had to wait in Hamburg for the ship, Malkele was very happy; but on board ship her mood had already changed. She began to long for her child, for her Yosele; day and night she talked only of Yosele, and she often wiped her eyes when she spoke of home.

They arrived in New York on 10 June 1910, but as soon as they got off the ship Malkele said to Dovid:

"I made a big mistake letting you talk me into going to America. I won't be able to stand it here without Yosele!"

She therefore soon met with her husband's brother and with other relatives of his. They had already had a letter from him that she had run away. She told them everything and showed them the marks on her body, which had not yet completely healed.

The family decided to bring her husband, Berman, to America and teach him here how to treat a wife. They wrote to him to that effect at once. At first he would not hear of travelling to that treyf America, but when they wrote to him that his wife would on no account come back, he softened and answered that he was coming with the child.

A few weeks later Reuven Berman arrived in America. The relatives reunited the couple and warned him to treat her well.

The new country had a good effect on Berman. Here he became a completely different man, and he began to treat Malkele like a true gentleman. He got a position here as a kashrut supervisor (mashgiach) and earned well; Malkele was now content.

Dovid would drop in at her home from time to time.

Why Is It Not Permitted to Trade in Fruit on Rybna Street? — A Statement by Vice-President Mr. Goetz [?]

For almost two weeks now the Magistrate [municipality] has not allowed the fruit stalls to be set up again [?] on Rybna Street.
In this connection we turned to the vice-president, Mr. Goetz [?], who gave the following statement.
"We have built market halls — says Mr. Goetz — on Modrzejowska [?] Street, where, in our opinion, the trade in fruit, greens etc. ought to be concentrated. When there were 2–3 stalls on Rybna Street, the Magistrate looked at it 'through its fingers'; but once the whole square was taken over by the fruit trade, which harmed the neighbouring shops that pay taxes and buy patents [trading licences] — that we cannot permit."
"What role did the Merchants' Union play in this matter?" we asked.
"The owners of the fruit shops, whom the street trade had harmed, turned to the Merchants' Union with a complaint, and the Merchants' Union sent the complaint on to the Magistrate. We hold — the vice-president added — that the Merchants' Union, as such, acted properly towards its members."

Because of "This" and "That" — the Patient Waited Three Days for the Medicine...

In the R. family a child is ill with a skin disease. On Monday Dr. Trapoyer [?] examined the child and wrote a prescription. At the pharmacy the patient was told that the prescription was illegible, and therefore the doctor should write it out again, more clearly. With that, Monday came to an end.
The next day Mr. R. came to the "Oberschlesien" [Upper Silesia — sick fund?], where the above-mentioned doctor rewrote the prescription.
When R. came for the medicine, the pharmacist again explained that since two medicines had been prescribed, each had to be on a separate prescription. Dr. T. would not agree to this, declaring that there is no such regulation that every medicine must be prescribed separately. The pharmacist said "yes" and the doctor "no", until Tuesday too had come to an end.
"And there was evening and there was morning, the fourth day": on Wednesday Mr. R. was already running with a [prescription?] to the manager of the "Oberschlesien" and laid before him the whole back-and-forth over the medicine for his sick child.

Seasonal workers' strike settled

On Monday some of the seasonal workers returned to work. The next day the strike was settled completely, and work is already proceeding normally.
— The occupation (sit-down) strike at the cable and wire factory had not ended as of Wednesday. The strike is proceeding calmly.
This Saturday — the Polish Soldier's holiday

On Tuesday, under the chairmanship of the starosta, Mr. Baksa [?], a meeting was held of the Zagłębie main committee for celebrating the “Soldier's Holiday”, which falls this Saturday, the 15th of this month, on the anniversary of halting the Bolshevik invasion in 1920.
The committee declared that the day of the 15th of this month should be a joyful holiday, on which various festivities are to take place.
In this spirit an appeal to the public will be issued.
Sosnowiec — Hooligan knocks out a young Jewish man's eye

On Monday night 18-year-old David Czarnocha was travelling from Katowice to Sosnowiec. In the same carriage there was also a Christian, who wanted to open a window in the carriage. Czarnocha did not allow him, explaining that one window was already open. The conductor agreed with this view too, and the second window was not opened.
The hooligan, however, took terrible revenge on Czarnocha, striking him in the street in Sosnowiec with a bottle above the eyes.
The result was terrible. The left eye was instantly almost completely destroyed. Czarnocha was taken to the Jewish hospital, where Dr. Horowitz performed the urgent operation.
Advocate Hofmokl-Ostrowski before the court in Sosnowiec

On the 25th of this month the trial of advocate Hofmokl-Ostrowski, defence counsel of Gruszczalski [?], will take place in the Sosnowiec municipal court.
Hofmokl-Ostrowski is charged with contempt of court.
The defendant applied for the trial not to be held in the municipal court; the proposal was rejected.
Petition of the Unemployed of Zagłębie for an Intervention by Rydz-Śmigły

[Zagłębie — unemployment, mines.]
Unemployed workers from Zagłębie have turned with a petition to the General Inspector of the Army, Gen. Rydz-Śmigły, in which they ask for an intervention in the matter of their getting work in the coal mines.
37 Sosnowiec Lawyers Will Defend Attorney Hofmokl-Ostrowski?

[Sosnowiec — courts.]
The Warsaw "Kurjer Czerwony" reports that 37 lawyers from Sosnowiec have volunteered to defend attorney Hofmokl-Ostrowski.
Among the lawyers there is also attorney Pawlak [?], who in Gruszeszalski's [?] trial appeared as an opponent of Adv. Hofmokl-Ostrowski.
"Linas Hacholim" Is Not Taking Part in the Kehilla Elections

[Sosnowiec — kehilla, elections, institutions.]
At the last meeting of the board of "Linas Hacholim" the question was discussed whether the institution should put up a separate list for the kehilla elections, in order to have its own representatives in the kehilla who would defend its interests.
Because the chairman, Mr. Goldkorn, declined to put up his candidacy, the board gave up putting up a separate list.
Professional Thief in the Role of a "Dentist"

[Sosnowiec — crime.]
A certain Klajnman from Kraków, already well known as a professional thief and burglar, has fallen into the hands of the local police. Klajnman, however, also has a weakness for the intelligentsia, and he introduces himself as a "dentist".
On this "bird" several quite new suits were found, which come from a theft.
The Court Is to Be Moved to New Premises

[Sosnowiec — municipality, courts.]
As we are informed, the municipal court, as well as the labour court, is being moved to the premises where the post office used to be. The work is already under way.
—o—
Two Victims in a "Biedaszyb"
[Vicinity — mines, accident.]
In the area of Psary, Łagisza commune, two workers were suffocated by gas in a "biedaszyb" [a primitive, illegal pit dug by the unemployed].
Dąbrowa — From the Election Front

[Dąbrowa — kehilla, elections.]
As was to be foreseen, in Dąbrowa there is a great abundance of... election lists. What Jewish "unity" looks like in reality is shown by the following figures:
In Dąbrowa there are 1308 persons entitled to vote, who are divided among 15 lists being put up. It is quite certain that if the number of voters were larger, the number of lists would reach as many as 20..
— The list of the Zionist Org. was changed at the last moment. Director Klein was to have figured in first place, but he withdrew, and in first place figures Prof. Steinberg.
— The artisans too could not come to an agreement, and 2 artisans' lists are being put up.
— For the first time a list of candidates of the worshippers of the shul is being put up, headed by Mr. Lipka-Puterka [?].
— A certain Hasid has applied to the election commission to strike from the voters' rolls 20 Radomsko Hasidim under paragraph 20.
Their "sin" consists in eating from the slaughtering of an unauthorized ("winkl") shochet.
The election commission rejected the proposal.
—o—
Suicide of a Jewish Girl
[Dąbrowa — suicide.]
On Monday 17-year-old Chana Welger went off to the "Zielona", where she drank a large dose of vinegar essence.
The suicide was taken in a serious condition to the Będzin hospital, where she died the next morning. The cause — a romantic one.
The Wild Dance of Demons around the Kehilla Elections

[Kielce — community.]
The united Jewish bloc torn apart because of a gang of seat-grabbers and careerists.
The united Jewish bloc for the kehilla elections in Kielce, which was to have been created on the initiative of Rabbi Rapoport, about which we already wrote in the last issue of our paper — has, to our greatest regret, not come about. For several days and nights people toiled to find some kind of formula for dividing the mandates among the political organizations, economic institutions and the non-party people. It was already almost certain that any moment now the bloc would be formed, but at the last minute nothing came of all the toil [?] and the united bloc was torn apart.
The first to renounce their participation in the general Jewish bloc were the "Poale Zion", who sent a written notice to the Kielce rabbi that, on the basis of the instructions they had received from the Warsaw Central Committee (C.C.), they must go to the elections with a separate list.
Then an attempt was made to create a united bloc of all the bourgeois organizations and associations together with the non-party people. The negotiations were conducted in a quite serious manner, so much so that the mandates had even [?] already been divided and people had already wished each other "mazel tov"; but in the end there came an invasion [?] of Hasidic shtiblekh, of insignificant prayer houses, as well as of various private seat-grabbers and plain careerists, who began to demand mandates categorically, with various threats. And since [?] there was not enough to go round, and there were more slaughterers than chickens, the unity bloc, having no choice, could no longer come about and had to be torn apart.
First of all came the Aleksander Hasidim and announced that under their leadership an association of a number of Hasidic shtiblekh had been formed, which lay claim to mandates. Otherwise they will put up a separate list.
Soon afterwards came the bootmakers' (gaiter-makers') guild; its representatives declared in turn that they are not going together with the general artisans' association, and that the association had not even negotiated with them. This guild too, which is actually a constituent part of the artisans' association, demanded separate mandates.
Later, further wild demands surfaced on the part of the economic organizations, such as the merchants' and the small traders' associations, concerning representation on the board, and so on and so forth.
Perhaps one might still somehow have managed, but then again surfaced an "unheard-of" proposal from certain groupings to disqualify, by legal and even [?] illegal means, the lists of the League and of the bootmakers' guild — to which the Zionist representatives would by no means agree, and they categorically opposed such shameful methods.
The only ones who truly wanted to bring about a unity bloc were the bourgeois Zionist groupings, which were willing to go to the most far-reaching compromises, just to avoid the disgusting election campaign.
Unfortunately it did not succeed, and the wild dance of demons around the kehilla elections has begun.
In the course of the week various conferences and consultations took place about creating various blocs. But each grouping keeps "as the secret of secrets" the various electoral machinations, which will become known precisely to the Jewish public only today, Friday, after the final deadline for submitting the candidate lists.
A piquant story about a certificate and a Christian mistress.

Mrs. Pesa Szyrławska [?] of Kielce tells an incredible story about her husband, an elderly man.
She has been living with her husband Chaim Yehoshua for 25 years now. He was a writing teacher in a cheder, made a good living, gave the children a good education, etc.
Three years ago they married off a daughter and gave her a quite decent dowry. The daughter and her husband left for Eretz Israel and in the course of time acquired a nice fortune there. The other 2 children are studying abroad.
Half a year ago the husband was dismissed from his post, and since then he would disappear from home for long periods. To her questions as to what had suddenly happened to him, he even began to beat her. She thought, however, that the change in him had come about because he had lost his post.
Two weeks ago she saw at his place a letter from the daughter, which spoke of his and her journey to Eretz Israel on the basis of a "drishe" [a relative's request for immigration]. Since he had not mentioned this whole Eretz Israel matter at all, it struck her as strange, and she began to investigate what was going on.
First she went to the cheder to find out why he had been dismissed from his post, and afterwards she questioned his acquaintances. There she learned that he has a Christian mistress, with whom he has been living for a long time, and since he had neglected his work in the cheder because of her, he had been dismissed from there and had received a larger sum of money as compensation.
Fearing that the scandal might become known in town, he thought it over and wrote to his daughter in Eretz Israel to send a "drishe" for him and his wife, intending to take the "kochanka" [mistress] there as his real wife. For this purpose he taught her Yiddish and everywhere introduced her as his wife.
Mrs. Pesa Szyrławska went at once to the starosta [district head] and handed him the whole matter. The starosta promised not to issue the husband a passport as long as the matter has not been thoroughly investigated. In addition, several respected householders turned to the Palestine Office with the request that it look into the matter closely and help the woman in her despair.
So far no "drishe" for him has arrived yet, but if a "drishe" does arrive, the Palestine Office will know how to act.
Zionists and Mizrachists go to the elections together.

In keeping with the long-standing tradition in Kielce, the Zionists and the Mizrachists, together with the General Zionists of Group B, are going to the kehilla elections together on a united list.
The news of a united Zionist and Mizrachi list, the so-called "Religious-National Electoral Bloc", aroused enormous satisfaction among almost the entire Jewish population of Kielce.
Fresh abuses in the Kielce magistrate.

During an inspection (lustration) of the various departments of the Kielce magistrate [municipality], it was established that the official of the registration office, the former alderman (ławnik) Jan Szyda [?], had committed abuses, demanding from applicants 4 and 5 zloty for issuing a passport, at a time when the fee amounts to only 70 groszy.
Szyda defended himself by saying that he had spent the difference in the sum on various documents that must be attached to the passport.
These abuses went on for a long time and were discovered only recently.
Szyda has been suspended from his post. As rumoured, he will be brought to account in court.
The Homeowners' Bank is being reorganised.

The council and management of the Homeowners' Bank have set about reorganising (restructuring) the bank. A reorganisation committee has been elected from the various strata of the Jewish population in Kielce.
The committee has set itself the task of granting low-interest credits to various merchants and small traders, who of late are being ruined even more by the lack of credit.
Bandit attack on a Jewish merchant.

In the village of Bicuty [?], Pińczów district, several armed bandits attacked the local merchant Yochanan Lemkowicz [?] in broad daylight and robbed him of 100 zloty.
The police are conducting a rigorous investigation.
A discount trip to Gdynia.

From the 15th to the 20th of this month there will be railway discounts to Gdynia. By buying a regular ticket to Gdynia and at the same time holding a confirmation, which is issued on the spot, one will receive a free ticket for the return journey.
On the eve of the opening of the theatre season in Kielce.

On 5 September the season of the Kielce-Radom theatre opens under the direction of Edward Czermański [?].
The ensemble, which has already been completed, consists of first-rank artistic forces, such as: Helena Bauszewska [?], S. Romacka [?], Wanda Libicka, Halina [?] Sudrażna [?], Maria Lejska [?], Messrs.: Jan Bielicz [?], Stefan Gałczewski [?], director Tomaszewski, St. Wszeszakiewicz [?], Warczykowski [?], M. Rembasz [?] and others.
The theatre season opens with the comedy "Klub kawalerów" [The Bachelors' Club].
At the second premiere "Muzyka na ulicy" [Music in the Street] will be staged.

Notes of the Week

The Arab terror in Palestine has again killed a large number of Jewish souls this week, among them several children. In Jaffa the state of emergency has been tightened; movement in the street is permitted for only three hours, daily from 5 to 8 in the morning.
—o—
Beyond Wilno a railway disaster occurred involving a passenger train; there are 2 dead and 17 injured.
—o—
At a summer resort near Czernowitz there were antisemitic incidents; the Jewish population was attacked with knives and sticks.
—o—
Beyond Radom there was a clash between Endeks and Polish workers; there are injured.
—o—
The World Jewish Congress closed in Geneva; Judge Julian Mack of America was elected honorary president of the Executive.
—o—
The French General Gamelin left Poland on the 16th of this month. Before his departure Gen. Gamelin was also received by the President at a breakfast.
A 70-year-old Jew forced to leave his village

The landowner Mr. Citer[?] of Pradła passes on the following fact to us:
In the village of Pradła lives the 70-year-old village peddler Yitzchok Rygski. The old man had lived in the village since his birth and got along with the local village population.
Then it so happened that the village of Pradła became a parish, and from then on hard days began for Rygski: at night the window panes of his home are smashed, and by day he and his family are harassed beyond endurance. Well, when the panes are smashed, one puts in new ones; but it became bitter when the roof was torn off the house in which he lived — then the old man took his family and settled in another village.
What's New in Upper Silesia?

Demonstrations.
On Sunday Endek demonstrations in honour of the "Miracle on the Vistula" took place in a number of towns across Upper Silesia. After the speeches a number of resolutions were adopted, among them that the Jewish question in Poland should be quickly solved by legal means such as: boycott, numerus clausus and support for emigration.
—o—
A theft.
Thieves, as yet undiscovered, broke into the flat of Asher Adler in Katowice. From there they stole jewellery worth 3,000 zł.
—o—
An explosion while cleaning floors with petrol.
In a flat on Lompy Street in Katowice a terrible accident happened through carelessness with petrol: the servants, after cleaning the floors with petrol, then used the "Electrolux" apparatus for cleaning; at a certain moment an explosion occurred, all the window panes in the flat were smashed, the doors torn open and the servants were nearly killed.
—o—
Motorcycle disaster.
Beyond Łagiewniki a motorcycle collided with a bicycle. The motorcyclist and his female companion were thrown off and seriously injured.
—o—
Accident during a firemen's drill.
During the drill of the Katowice firemen a firemen's wagon overturned, and of them[?] several were injured.
—o—
Government order.
The Ministry of Railways has ordered rails from the "Piłsudski" steelworks for a sum of 300,000 zł., and also iron for 100,000 zł.
—o—
Cut up alive.
A gruesome accident happened on Friday evening at the brickworks of Dr. Jakubowicz in Mikołów. During work the press machine caught a woman worker, who was cut to pieces.
—o—
"The Romanian Wedding" in Chorzów.
Next Monday the Jewish troupe of the Łódź "Philharmonia" is guesting in Chorzów; the well-known operetta "The Romanian Wedding" was[?] performed.

Festive prayer in the Katowice synagogue.
In connection with the "Day of the Polish Soldier" a festive divine service was held in the Katowice synagogue on Sabbath after prayers, with the participation of Rabbi Chameides, who delivered a speech on topics of the day.

Katowice kehilla for the "FAM" [?].
At the last meeting of the kehilla board in Katowice 500 zł. were assigned for the benefit of the Polish air-defence fleet.

A tenants' meeting.
A meeting of the tenants' associations of the entire Silesian Voivodeship was held in Katowice.
A lengthy lecture pointed to the latest decree of the President of the State on reducing rents.
After the discussion of the lecture resolutions were adopted, among them that the decree on cheaper rent should also cover business premises.

On the 17th of this month the drawing of the third class of the thirty-sixth State Lottery ended. The three main prizes of a hundred thousand zł. each fell this time in three provincial towns, and fortune was especially friendly to those whom it had long forgotten.

On this occasion we mention that on the 27th of this month[?] the supplementary "after-..."[?] drawing took place among the tickets that remained in the wheel after the end of the drawing of the 4th class of the thirty-fifth lottery and on which no premium prizes had been awarded in the drawing.
When one doesn't hold one's tongue between one's teeth...

An interesting trial took place these days before the District Court in Sosnowiec.
In the dock sat Mrs. Rivka Wodzisławska, who had been brought to court for accusing the lawyer Pardistal[?] of Będzin of having supposedly told her that "without a bribe for the judges you don't win a case".
The investigation into this proved that she had simply accused the lawyer falsely, and for that she was sentenced to four months' arrest.
No kehilla elections will take place in Zawiercie. A united bloc of all parties.

On Tuesday the last meeting of all the organizations took place with the participation of the Rabbi (may he live long and happily), who in a speech prevailed upon all the parties not to allow Jewish unity to be broken at so difficult a time. Having heard the speech, all undertook[?] to act in accord[?] with the Rabbi, and it was unanimously resolved that only one united list would remain, representing all the parties.
Since no second list was submitted, no elections will take place. This is the only town in Zagłębie that has shown understanding for a bloc.

A man in the role of a midwife.

In the village of Rudnik, Zawiercie district, a peasant woman gave birth. Her husband, however, did not call any midwife for his sick wife, not even a "babka" [folk midwife], but performed the work of midwifery himself.
The result was fatal. A few hours after the birth the woman in childbed died.
The police are conducting an inquiry into the reasons why the man did not call a doctor to his sick wife.

What Shall We Do with Our Children?

This very question we hear at every step from parents whose children have finished the elementary schools.
The question naturally does not exist for well-to-do parents (a very thin stratum nowadays). For them the answer is clear — the gymnasium. They do not even have the time to let their children finish elementary school. Already from the fifth grade, or even from the fourth (often in the middle of the school year), the child is taken out of school and crammed "by force" for the gymnasium. There is no time — faster, faster! (just as if posts for doctors and lawyers were standing and waiting for them), and no attention is paid to the fact that the child is thereby broken. One forces one's way from one stage of development into the next, and the child is not allowed to receive a complete, finished, systematic education.
In all its sharpness the above-mentioned question — what to do with the children who have finished elementary school — confronts the broad masses of the people, and that for two reasons. First and foremost — the material situation: there is nothing to pay with! Most parents have not the slightest possibility of giving their children higher education; and besides, the former drive of the Jewish bourgeoisie towards higher education after secondary school has already weakened — which used to mean securing oneself materially. Who did not once dream that his child would become a lawyer, a doctor, that is, a person with a secure livelihood, and on top of that the prestige, the honour of it...
Today the situation is different. Here the children of Chaim, of Moshe, of Grunem finished their matura long ago, and even university, and now "graze" the streets. They have nothing to do, and at best one gets a private lesson for 8 gulden [złoty] a month.
Education today is no longer any remedy for obtaining work of any kind, employment, let alone for making a position for oneself in life. It no longer pays; all the efforts and agonies spent on getting the matura, on getting into university etc., do not pay, because — what comes afterwards?!!
So what remains for us to do with the young people? Some go to become clerks, bookkeepers etc.; about the practicality and purpose of such a way out it is superfluous even to waste a word. And what then? The greater part goes, and must go — into a trade. Despite all the unemployment and the difficulty of finding work even for skilled tradesmen, learning a trade is still the best way out for the greater part of our youth. The socio-economic development of society is leading to a point where only the well-qualified tradesman will be able to hold a position and a place in life.
And here we come to a second important question: the "well-qualified tradesman". If this is so[?] in general, then Jewish handicraft is the field that most needs good, qualified forces. For only such a craftsman, who will be the best qualified, still has any chance at all of withstanding the intensifying struggle against him.
How is this achieved — how do we see to it that the young person who goes into a craft trains professionally, becomes qualified and does not come out a cripple? With the master, even a qualified one, one cannot learn the trade thoroughly, either theoretically or practically.
The best way out would be to found a network of vocational schools, and with today's article we are indeed aiming at a practical purpose. It does not occur to us to write just like that, for the sake of writing.
What can actually be done in this field is to found vocational courses, where the apprentice who is learning with a master, or intends to learn, will receive everything that the master cannot give him in professional training and general development.
Founding such courses will not be hard to carry out in practice. And such courses can easily turn into a vocational school in time.
This task should be taken on by the "ORT" branch, which was in fact created for such things.
May our appeal this time not remain a voice crying in the wilderness, as is already the custom with us.
A. Mem.
Jewish Trade and Antisemitism

Jewish trade in Poland, and especially the small trader, has now been placed in danger; Endek antisemitism has taken him on in an entirely different way.
Until now "swój do swego" ["each to his own" — the Endek boycott slogan] was preached in theory; now it is also being turned into practice.
Now the slogan is no longer: "Buy from your own!" Now it is: if there are no "own people" on the spot, one must create one — anything so as not to buy from the Jew.
And this "own man" must be created whether he likes it or not — even if he has no wish for it[?]. Out of "patriotism" he must set himself up in the market with a stall of goods, although he has no knowledge of it whatsoever.
Even if the peasant does not want it, he is forced to turn from a peasant into a trader — anything to push out the Jew.
In the small towns the markets are being moved far from the Jewish dwelling houses and from the Jewish shops. The peasant who comes to market should thus have no opportunity even to get a whiff of a Jewish shopkeeper.
That is how the situation of Jewish trade actually stands now.
We will not go here into the causes and aims of the new transformation that the new Endek antisemitism in Poland has undergone; that would lead us too far. Let us speak about the fact as it is.
And the fact is a very threatening one for Jewish trade.
So what remains to be done in such a situation?
It is clear, and there can be no two opinions about it, that in awareness of the danger it becomes even more necessary for Jewish small traders to fuse together into an even firmer and stronger organisation; with united forces one can resist the danger more easily than when each fights separately for himself.
Never before has it been so convincing that only in unity can one save oneself from ruin. Frictions and quarrels must now step aside. The Jewish small trader must now become an armoured body, so as to be able to protect himself from all the arrows aimed at him by Endek antisemitism in Poland.
If the small trader understands now, in the hour of danger, how to guard his common interests, then the bullets fired at his body will bounce back.
The methods of self-defence for Jewish small trade against the antisemitic attacks, the means of defending oneself against the Endek offensive on the positions of Jewish trade in general and Jewish small trade in particular, will surely be found, we believe, by the relevant small traders' organisations in the localities where they are active. This must also be, first and foremost, the task of the representative bodies and of the representatives of the small traders in all the other institutions where they are represented: town councils, chambers of commerce, kehillas, etc.
Let us hope that Jewish small trade will withstand the antisemitic danger that lies in wait for Jewish livelihoods. Let us hope that it will manage to come out of the wild Endek war in peace, and that it will outlive Endekism in general and antisemitism in particular.
A. J. G—ski.
Ciechocinek (A Miniature Reportage). (2)

P. Blumenkranc (Ciechocinek).
1. Dancing.
The burden in Ciechocinek — as in all spa resorts — is the baths; the main pleasure — dancing.
Old bachelors with bald patches, who at home have their heads in a spin over bills of exchange and their years [?] twisted on account of their wives, let themselves go wild here; every day they crawl to the dancing master, where to a hoarse gramophone they shuffle their feet for half an hour, and in the afternoon it is back to the pool.
Ciechocinek already has dance heroes of the kind who for decades have been shuffling their feet to the sounds of a hoarse gramophone and in the evening tread on their partners' corns. And so it goes, year after year. Apparently the angel gives them, as they leave Ciechocinek, a flick [?] on the nose or the foot, and all the wisdom they have learned flees in the blink of an eye.
But dance one must. It is a categorical imperative, and in any case, between ourselves, there is no difference at all between a good dancer and a "shuffler", because nobody can do more than shuffle his feet, owing to the crush and the shoving.
The good dancer therefore comes early, and while the crowd has not yet gathered he spreads himself out in the English waltz, dances a sentimental tango and cuts figures in the slow-fox to his heart's content.
But his joy does not last long: the young "cripples" and the old shufflers soon gather, and when Gold launches [?] into the tango:
"Ostatnia niedziela, dziś się rozstaniemy" ["The last Sunday, today we shall part"], all the old women smile — the ones who remember a waltz from their young years — and hop a waltz mixed with a polka to the tango music. Elderly people who learned a foxtrot in a hurry run through the tango "foxtrot-style".
But it makes no difference — (in the crush, in the jostling] nobody notices any of this. It is enough that the "orangeade" stands on the little table with a pierced [?] straw, and he, who all year long has troubles upon troubles and scenes of jealousy from his "accursed one" [?], holds in his arms before all eyes a strange woman, who smiles at him as his wife — only good be said of her today [?] — did at their engagement. He smiles and tangles his feet, steeped in sweat as after a hot bath, until Gold gets tired. Then, sighing with relief, he kisses, all sweaty, the damp [?] hand of his "Julia" and, with a sigh of contentment, goes back to sit down [?].
It is all worth it — just not to look at the "old woman"...
2. Women.
As is well known, everywhere there are more women than "free" [?] men: in one place 106 to a hundred, in another — 110 to a hundred, and in the spa resorts — perhaps 130 to 100.
But as many women — no evil eye — as Ciechocinek has, there surely are in no country and no Polish spa (not even Krynica).
What do you mean, women! Simply: "and seven women shall take hold of one man" [Isaiah 4:1]. The young men were so confused by the great abundance that they started taking walks by themselves.
And what is worse [?]: because of the large choice they have become outlandish connoisseurs and turn up their noses, like — to make the distinction — a Jewish daughter who has bought herself a doctor for a husband...
So I witness five women who want to go to "Pod Mieżan" [?] (a café) and have one male person between them; a Warsaw woman [?] objects, she does not want to go [?] on terms of three persons:
— Excuse me [?], I came with a partner, and for us it "is not proper" [wypada] that five "women" [niewiasty] should sit with one "man" [mężczyzna] — I absolutely do not agree! [stanowczo się nie zgadzam]
The second one parries [?]:
— Pani wybaczy, ten pan jest moim znajomym! ["Excuse me, madam, this gentleman is my acquaintance!"]
And then the third with a complaint, and later the fourth.
In short, I won't tell you the whole story, because the main thing is the ending, and truly, by a miracle, one of them had a tremendous [?] idea, and at once [?]: they remembered that they had one more acquaintance — an old man, true, who cannot even shuffle his feet in a crush, but now it is "proper" in a different way: 2 to 5 is, after all, not one to 5.
The proposal was adopted by acclamation, and with joy and gladness they went to fetch [?] the grey [?] bachelor-bridegroom, who was busy resting his rheumatic feet and was about to undress [?].
Two women took the old fellow by the arm and sat him down in the open-air café, so that he thought something would happen to him from the cold. He shivered and sipped the cold tea, and the next morning all five women told their "znajome" [lady friends] how they had had a "świetnie" [splendid] time, how the "stary" [old] acquaintance is "dowcipny" [witty] and "staroświecki" [old-fashioned] [?]...
3. The dream of the naive [?].
The assimilationists of former days — among whom there were undoubtedly many honest, truly well-meaning people — thought in their naivety that when a Jew showed the gentiles that he was honest, useful, capable, the gentiles would become lovers of Israel and would come to love [him].
So one of them, Wawelberg by name, built a technical school in Warsaw. The school exists (it has even risen higher), but Jews are driven out of there with sticks, as everywhere else.
That same Wawelberg founded a colony in Ciechocinek where every season [?] (month) 180 poor children stay, regardless of faith. Even the staff is mixed: Jewish and Christian personnel.
Very fine! A truly beautiful idea. Every person who suffers must be helped, and all the more so children, who are just beginning to take their first steps in life, these innocent little souls, who should pass their days in joy; and needless to say, when it comes to poor children whom want has crippled, one must surely, surely hurry to help, regardless of how the other prays and to whom.
And when I indeed saw Jewish and Christian children playing, strolling and dancing about together, I felt somehow cosier; I was already on the point of beginning to believe that man is good by nature — and [—] [?]...
But this joy of mine was disturbed in the middle. I am standing there as a group of children goes out for a walk: a Jewish boy, a shrivelled little thing, with a big patch on his cloth trousers, holds on to another; his little legs are weak, so he leans on his friend.
Suddenly he gets a shove. A fair-haired "shaygetsl" [gentile boy] pushes him and bellows:
— Żydusie, Żydusie! [?] [roughly "little Yid"]
The shaygetsl looked at him with such burning anger, like an Endek student. The little boy looked around frightened and bewildered and did not know what to answer.
And I, poor man, was jolted awake again by this little episode: so it means that the doctrine of the grown-ups has penetrated so deeply into the small fry that even when the morsel, the Jewish one, is in your mouth, you need not keep even the form of gratitude.
We, the few, need no proofs that we shall not convince our enemies. Today they shout openly not only "neither your sting nor your honey", but that they do not want even the [?] honey...
But how great would the disappointment of such a Wawelberg have been! One feels pity for the naivety of these honest people.
Our Lawless World

[Article — the lawless world; Palestine and the British Mandate.]
We live in a lawless world; we breathe falsification and are fed on “clear lies”.
Wherever one turns and wherever one looks — everywhere the same atmosphere of wild lawlessness, deceit and mendacity.
It makes no difference in what circle you move and to which corner of life you give your attention, be it the upper world or be it the underworld — everywhere you find the same measure of lawlessness and falsification and lies, in deeds and in conduct; everywhere all possible obligations have been abolished, a word is no word, an amen [?] is no amen.
Whether it concerns relations between nation and nation or between man and man.
People laugh impudently at those who demand honesty, mock those who remember yesterday's moral values, and turn away from those who insist on decency.
And not only individual by individual, country by country, community by community, each taken by itself, leads a lawless life or a lawless politics — but all countries and nations taken together, as one whole body — just as the “League of Nations” presents it — are one great reprobate, one wild lawless lad who is enraptured by the heavy fist and sings “hallelujahs” to the robbery and the murder that flood the world.
The whole world suffers from this state of affairs; tens of millions of people and more are crushed and ground down by the boundless lawlessness — but more lawlessly, more shamefully and more mercilessly it touches us, the Jews, and everywhere:
in Europe as in Asia, in Africa as in America.
Everywhere the reprobates stand in camps, in millions, and demand our destruction. Why? To that they answer with “all sorts of” opinions — not merely false, but falsified, deliberately falsified — and these are even “interpreted”... with “all sorts of” quotations and lampoons, about which not only the readers but, what is more, the writers themselves are convinced that everything written there is a hundred percent and more lies through and through — and yet they are received with a feigned seriousness.
Well, and what happens with the thousands of lying lampoon-writers and with the tens of thousands of insolent lampoon-spreaders everywhere, as wide as the world is? Have those who are able to interfere interfered with it? Have the strong and mighty of the world applied their power and used their strength not to allow lawlessness, which is truly a mortal danger, to spread freely and openly over the world?
And what has the League of Nations done, seeing the terrifying growth of lawlessness and the brutalization of the world and its people? What has the League of Nations undertaken against the wildly screaming poisoning of the world and its sinking into an abyss of lies and blood libel and intrigue and incitement of lawlessness? Has it [?] uttered even a single word against the millions of wood-carriers and coal-shovellers to that hellfire in which we are so mercilessly burned and roasted?
And what is England doing about its share of the lawlessness, and what is France doing about its black, bloody share? And what is the United States doing against the wild offshoots of lawlessness and lies?
And what are the other, smaller states of the world doing — where they do not directly help the growth and spread of the plague — against the lawlessness and mendacity that rule them?
The smaller ones like the bigger ones — they do nothing. With the patience of the ancient Stoics they sit and look on calmly and undisturbed as lawlessness spreads, as the lie [printed “der ligent”] has the great say and poisons the world.
And in times of danger, doing nothing against it is a reinforcement of it. By not putting out a fire one gives it more power [printed “nit” for “git”], one enlarges the bounds of its possible devastation.
And this letting the danger stand [?] by not opposing it, this strengthening of the influence of lies and falsification in the life of nations, by pretending not to know what is happening all around — this is the great sin of the few, better governments that we can count in the world.
If the world suffers from this mendacious state of affairs, the Jews suffer along with it. But we Jews, being what we are, must keep a double bookkeeping: one — for our bloody business in partnership with the world, and a second — for our special sufferings, for the special lies and incitements of the world concerning us.
Let us limit ourselves this time to our special field. We leave aside the world and the Jews of the world, with the incitements and lies of the world against us. We want to dwell only on our homeland.
And here too we do not want to take up all the material of incitement; here too we leave aside the incitements and lies and intrigues that our enemies carry on around us, and we dwell only on the lies and the falsifications that our so-called friends — the English officialdom — spread against us in the country. That alone is enough to include the government of our homeland within the bounds of the general “lawless world”.
For ever since the country became restless, ever since Arabs began to slaughter and murder — as is their wont — the representatives of the government in the Land of Israel have begun to fabricate false reports about the course of the bloody events. The world and the people knew that it was not the Jews who began the murder, but, relying on special reports from Jerusalem, the Colonial Secretary in London specially announced a “clash” between Jews and Arabs — as though Jews too had taken part in the murders, which is an open lie. Later the new Colonial Secretary came and added a fresh couple of lies: also relying on the falsified reports from Jerusalem, he gave Parliament the number of arrested Arabs and Jews since the murders began; in doing so, however, they forgot to state that the Jews had been arrested because they were out of their houses after the forbidden hour [the curfew], while the Arabs were arrested for murder.
And one thing more: the world and the people know the responsible leaders of the murderous Arab strike, yet the London government, relying on the lying reports of the Jerusalem government, has asserted that the Arab pogrom leadership is innocent here — because it has lost its influence over the pogrom gang.
And more, and more, and more...
Thus the falsification grows and the lies grow; incitement, intrigue and lawlessness spread in our homeland as in the un-homely countries.
And there is no power in the world, neither single nor united, that would stand up against the dangerous plague of lies and lawlessness in which the world is sinking.
Are we indeed already standing at the end of the world?..
Jewish Children from Sosnowiec at the Colony in Andrychów

[Sosnowiec — welfare; summer colony.] At the summer colony in Andrychów organized by the Sosnowiec "Dobroczynność" [Charity] society, headed by its president Dr. Herzman, 141 poor Jewish children from Sosnowiec spent 5 happy weeks.
The colony was housed in the building of the local public school and occupied 5 comfortable bedrooms, a large dining hall, a kitchen, etc.
A splendid view spread out from the windows of the colony building. In the distance one saw the beautiful Beskid mountains covered with dense fir[?] trees, near the stream Wieprzówka with the famous Andrychów swimming pool. Great interest in the colony was shown by the head of the local public school, Mr. Józef Gwakowski[?].
The local Jewish population also presented the children with gifts with much sympathy; special thanks are owed to: the local kehilla president Dr. Lewicz[?], Rabbi Dawid Awigdor, and the doctors Messinger, Zeilender, Ogarowanski[?], as well as the dentist H. Mandrer[?], who supervised the health of the colony.
Thanks to the uncommon abilities and devotion of the colony director, Mr. Aleksander Krupe[?] (teacher at Public School No. 8 in Sosnowiec), and the 2 educators, the Misses F. Treisman and J. Majerczyk[?], the children spend the day happily. It begins at 7 o'clock in the morning, then 10 minutes of gymnastics under the open sky, afterwards washing, and at 8.40 breakfast; then the children march out singing to the nearby mountain covered with green fields and woods, "Pańska[?] Góra", where they spend the time playing until noon; after lunch they rest 2 hours until "Vesper" [the afternoon snack], afterwards a walk or bathing at the beach[?] until supper. At 8.30 the colony is already sunk in deep sleep.
The good air and the sun make the children's appetite rise. Travelling[?] home, they cast longing glances at the mountains they are leaving, with filled-out, round, darkly tanned bodies and faces. It is only to be regretted that Jewish Sosnowiec did not find enough means to send out a second, similar group of poor children.
We believe, however, that next year this shortcoming will be remedied.
Andrychów, July—August 1936.
Election Hodgepodge

[Feuilleton — kehilla elections; Sosnowiec, Dąbrowa, Będzin.] Overheard by Sh. Libaszon[?].
Sixteen days younger...
Don't get upset over the bad tidings that the Jewish press serves you from "our" Altneuland; don't fall into a despairing mood because the number of victims there grows from day to day, for these are trifles. So what's the use[?] of talking about them and stirring up[?] more heartache? — Certainly, certainly not, because [—][?] by our duty, there are still enough matters on which our fate, our existence and our pride in the eyes of the nations depend.
The town of Będzin has this time been excluded from the rule — being the only town in Poland that has not had the privilege of dancing at the general election-wedding, and one must, poor things, make do with writing "wyjaśnienia" [explanations] to the starostwo [district office], [protests?] and installing[?] presidents, and supplying reports to the antisemitic press about the gmilus-khesed fund and about the kehilla...
Quite different, however, is the situation in the towns "in front"[?] and "behind" — Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa. In these towns the mood of the Jewish population is a proud one: heads held high, "beaming"[?] faces, carefree — and why not, indeed?
— "After all, we're on the eve of kehilla elections"!!
And scribes write and strike out, auditors[?] check the birth certificates of every candidate — whether it is exact and certain that So-and-so son of So-and-so, the future parnas, is already a full 30 years old, if he was born before 12 at night, or at twilight...
And here is what my own ears heard:
Into the office of the election commission for the Sosnowiec kehilla elections comes a representative of the "Agudah" — by the way a clever Jew — who innocently puts the following question to the commission's secretary:
— Tell me, I beg you, sir... when, for instance, was the candidate on this or that list born; is he really already a full 30 years old? It's hard to believe; please take the trouble and check.
And after the secretary granted the request and checked exactly when Yekl son of Shmerl, the future dozór member [board member] of the holy community of Sosnowiec, descended into this sinful world, it indeed turned out that Yekl son of Shmerl is barely 29 years and three hundred and 44 days old, that is, he is short a whole 16 days of 30 years...
The "[?]" breathed the breath of life into the Agudah leader; his cheeks reddened with joy over the discovered "theft"...
— Ha—ha—ha — he burst out laughing — who besides me would come up with such a brilliant[?] idea, to check whether the "youngster"[?] is already 30 years old — his innards rejoice[?]
And with a smiling face he left the kehilla office, and already standing on the threshold he asked once more, to be sure:
— Sixteen days younger?...
Happy are you, O Israel...
"The culture of a nation is recognised by its soap consumption," a minister once said — and we say that in the correspondence in the possession of the election commission in Dąbrowa, the face of the Dąbrowa kehilla is mirrored.
We are truly "grateful" to the chairman of the election commission of the holy community of Dąbrowa, who is known as courteous and enlightened, for letting us acquaint ourselves with the correspondence, and even more grateful are we to the creators of the election regulations, in which paragraph 20 is found.
— Oh, what a wild paragraph that is! I swear to you by beard and sidelocks. A hundred "Agudas HaRabonim", even together with the Będzin "Committee for Kashrut and Strengthening of Torah", are not capable of strengthening "Jewishness" the way this single, kind-hearted little paragraph does... Every single one who merely has it in mind to get into the kehilla takes care not to transgress the smallest prohibition, the slightest little sin; a trembling seizes everyone when he remembers that such a paragraph is found in the "little prayer-book"; even the chairman of the election commission, God forbid, won't take a bite of breakfast until his head is covered with a hat...
But this we have remarked in passing, by the way. Yes, where were we — at the correspondence. A very[?] rich correspondence. Rare materials for the museum of "YIVO" — a pity, upon my life, that such a "treasure" should go to waste and not be preserved for the future historian.
Most "interesting" of all is that the "writers" are not from opposing camps but of "one flesh and blood".
Here we read how the Artisans' Association informs the election commission that the tailor Tsan[?], who wants to "make Shabbes for himself", was caught in the "act" and his hands must be examined...
A second letter "relates" that "the candidates on the rabbi's list are adherents of the 'love that depends on a thing'"... But then the head[?] of the rabbi's list comes and declares that this is a simple slander and that the hatred of the list is simply out of envy, because the whole town is waiting for the honest parnasim who figure on his list.
We read a third and a fourth "letter" from the "rich" correspondence, after which one feels like crying out:
"How fortunate you are, Jews of Dąbrowa, how good it is for you that you have had the privilege of being among the 'fortunate' towns that practise the laws of elections, and need not waste[?] your time, nor lose any strength reading the 'foolish' news about the Jewish situation in the whole world in general and in the Land of Israel in particular...
— Happy are you, O Israel!
Fools, Simpletons, Strange Characters.

[Feuilleton — strange collectors; followed by a news item: film.]
We who live on this side of Europe know very little of that breed of strange collectors who spend all their money and wealth collecting the most varied objects from all over the world. At most we know of stamp collectors or coin collectors, but who, for instance, knew that the former Spanish king Alfonso collected matchboxes all his life, or who knows, for instance, that the well-known millionaire Yault[?] Smith of Chicago has been collecting trouser buttons all his life; he already has the buttons of generals and of the American presidents Washington and Kramvelli[?] and of more and more great men...
The Argentine millionaire Gonzales collects all kinds of instruments with which a person was killed. The axe with which Louis XVI's head was chopped off he bought [?] at a precious price... His collection even contains the knife with which Brutus stabbed Caesar; all he lacks is the stone with which Cain killed Abel and the little stone[?] with which David killed Goliath..
Some 20 years ago the London millionaire William Watson sold at the Leipzig fair a collection of tram, ship and railway tickets from all over the world. An American paid a fortune for the collection at the time; nevertheless Watson did not get even a tenth of what the collection had cost him.
Mister Morrison of Nebraska (South America). Keeps every kind of cigarette and cigar that exists in the world. Special agents in all countries send him every new brand that appears anywhere on the market.
In Liverpool there is a rich woman, Mrs. Welham[?], who collects earth from all the cemeteries of the whole world; she pours the earth onto her grave, which she bought for herself in her lifetime, so that when she dies she will lie in a cemetery from the four corners of the earth.
In Boston there exists a society of [?] strange collectors; each of the members collects something different: one collects teeth, another shoes, a third hats and a fourth umbrellas.
One of them collects water from all the rivers and seas of the whole world; the bottles stand on display at his home and on each little bottle it is written exactly where the water comes from.
One collects paper soldiers; among them there is one who collects every kind of tinned food that exists, no matter what is in the tin. With his collection he could feed thousands of people for months, although many of the tins are already old and no longer fit to eat.
Mrs. Dougherty of Manchester collects the signatures of women who have had at least five husbands... She already has a sizable bundle of such signatures; she herself has been widowed 8 times and divorced 3 times..
Mrs. Andrey of London collects love letters from girls no older than 17. She then reads the letters day and night.
Quite a large share of strange collectors have devoted themselves to all kinds of clothing.
About them[?] — another time.
Z. Haber, Vienna.

Gitel Gutman, of blessed memory (A few words at the fresh grave)

The Jewish community of Będzin lost this week one of its most popular women, a communal worker, a philanthropist in the full sense of the word — the noble Mrs. Gustawa Gutman, of blessed memory.
With the loss of Mrs. Gutman the whole of public Jewish Będzin is in mourning; great and small, young and old bewail the heavy loss of one of whom it may be said: "Alas for those who are gone and are not forgotten!"
Quietly and modestly she fulfilled her duties in the Jewish and humane spirit; with a generous hand she supported respectable people of Będzin and the surrounding area who had come down in the world.
She supported all Jewish and public institutions, and also all religious establishments.
Whoever turned to her for help received an immediate response. She helped with large sums to set up the orphanage; significant[?] were her commitments to the old-age home and to Linat Holim; she arranged weddings for poor brides — and all of it so modestly, quietly, so delicately, that nobody should know of it, without publicity, without any announcement even in the press...
The deceased was a very good mother, a true patroness in the deepest sense of the Jewish spirit.
The husband has lost the best of wives, the children the best of mothers, and Jewish society one of its greatest philanthropic pillars.
We always mourn the death of gifted[?] people in the field of literature and art, but even more is to be mourned the death of a person who sustained the livelihood and dignity of hundreds of families.
It remains to hope, however, that the departed Mrs. Gutman will serve as an example to those who remain, and that she will remain immortal in the history of Będzin's Jewish public life.
The imposing funeral was a sign of her merits.
Peace to her dust! May the earth lie lightly on her!
H. Szer.
—o—
The entire Jewish population of Będzin received with grief, last Saturday night, the news that Gitel Gutman, wife of the well-known philanthropist Mr. Jakub Gutman, had died. Hundreds of people gathered in front of the Gutmans' house and did not stop recounting the praises and virtues of the deceased.
On Sunday at 10 a.m. the board of the "Orphanage" held an urgent mourning session; the chairman, Dr. Weinzieher, opened the session with a short memorial speech in which he pointed out the magnitude of the loss. After the deceased had been honoured with a minute's silence, a number of points were discussed concerning participation in the funeral and how the society should perpetuate the name of the late Mrs. Gutman.
It was resolved: 1) the whole board attends the funeral as one man; 2) a group of children shall carry during the funeral a banner with a fitting inscription; 3) in the large hall named after the Gutman family the portraits of the deceased and of her husband, Mr. Jakub Gutman, shall be hung in medallion form; and 4) on the day of the shloshim a memorial assembly shall be held in the orphanage.
The funeral took place at 3 p.m., but already an hour earlier thousands of people from all strata of the Jewish population had gathered in Kołłątaja Street. The crush was so great that a fairly large group from "Hakoach" could not master the situation and keep proper order.
From minute to minute the number of mourners grew, among them a large number of delegations, among others from Fürstenberg's gymnasium, the Zionist organisation, "Keren Kayemet", "Keren Hayesod", "Hiyush"[?], "Hakoach", "Linat Holim", "Beit Lechem", etc.
The coffin with the dead was set down in the courtyard, and Rabbi Friedberg in his eulogy described the great loss Jewish society had suffered through the death of Mrs. Gutman, who was a great benefactress and possessed a warm Jewish heart.
The funeral procession moves off; behind the coffin walks the family, then delegations, among them children of the orphanage carrying a silk ribbon with the inscription: "A monument to a dear soul — Gitel Gutman, of blessed memory", and many thousands of people who accompanied the dead to the cemetery.
In front of the purification house Rabbi Hager of Sosnowiec delivered a eulogy rich in content that left an unforgettable impression. Through various sayings of the Sages Rabbi Hager pointed to the noble[?] figure of the deceased, who, although she lived in rich and modern surroundings, nevertheless remained faithful to the Jewish religion and to ideal Jewish traditions; she embodied "She stretches out her hand to the poor, and reaches forth her hands to the needy" (Prov. 31:20), giving with a generous hand to every poor man and also sending large donations to impoverished homes[?].
The cantor Mr. Klagsbald[?] with the choir sing a chapter of Psalms, "Yoshev beseter" (Ps. 91), and the coffin is carried out to the grave, where Dr. Weinzieher, in the name of "Dobroczynność" ("Charity"), delivered a moving eulogy that brought forth weeping in the family and also among the large crowd of mourners.
Dr. Weinzieher said that the deceased had been the Jewish matron, a model wife for her husband and mother for her children; she brought harmony into her family life and was the guide of her entire family.
After the "El Male" the sons say Kaddish, and the thousand-headed crowd leaves the fresh, flower-adorned grave. May her soul be bound up in the bond of life.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Shoftim)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Shoftim
—o—
a) "You shall not plant yourself an Asherah" (Deut. 16:21)
"Whoever appoints an unworthy judge is as if he planted an Asherah."
Why is an "unworthy judge" compared to an Asherah? Because all kinds of idols are recognised at once by their outward appearance as being idols. They are images of the gods whom the misguided worship. An Asherah, however, is a tree like other trees, blooming [?], with beautiful green branches — and yet it is an idol. So too with an "unworthy judge": outwardly nothing at all can be recognised in him. A Jew in a shtreimel, a rabbi — and yet he can be an idol... Melo ha-Omer.
—o—
b) "And to the judge who shall be in those days" (Deut. 17:9)
"...You have only the judge of your own days." Rashi.
People complain that judges and leaders today are smaller than they once were, and forget that the generations too are smaller. "Do not say that the former days were better than these, for it is not out of wisdom that you ask this." That the former days were better than today's, that they had [?] better leaders — "it is not out of wisdom that you ask": this shows your lack of wisdom, the decline of the generation... Penei Yafot.
—o—
c) "You shall not turn aside from the word which they tell you, right or left"
"Even if he tells you of right that it is left, and of left that it is right." Rashi.
The Rebbe of Kock once [?] explained a path in Hasidism to a Hasid. But according to that man's understanding it came out exactly the opposite. Seeing [?] this, the Kotzker says to him:
"Go call Itche Meir (the author of Chiddushei ha-Rim) — there he is in the beit midrash, on the right."
The Hasid looks for him on the right and comes back with nothing; he did not find him there.
"Ox!" the Kotzker rages in his manner. "When I told you 'on the right', I meant right as seen from me, by my right hand. What is right for me comes out left for you..."
And he pulled [?] the Hasid by the ear: from now on you will know "even if he tells you of right that it is left and of left that it is right", because what you call left is in truth right..
—o—
d) "That he may learn to fear... that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren" (ibid., v. 20)
Our leaders allow themselves to lord it over the public not for the sake of Heaven, because — so they prove from the sayings of the Sages — a leader must, after all, have an eighth of an eighth of pride, so that people should respect him, so that he can hold the community in hand [?].
In truth there is another way to evoke reverence among the masses: sincere piety, true fear of Heaven — "And all the peoples of the earth shall see that the name of the Lord is called upon you, and they shall be afraid of you". And this is what the verse says: "that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren", so that he need not act grand. So that he need not display pride in order to be respected, there is a way: "that he may learn to fear" — let him display fear of Heaven, honest piety, and that will evoke respect for him. Ma'adanei Melech.
—o—
e) "You shall be wholehearted with the Lord your God" (Deut. 18:13)
Live always at peace with God: even when He is good to you, be good to Him too. For mostly a man is good to God when God is bad to him... And this is what we pray: "Let Your kindness, O Lord, be upon us, as we have hoped for You." Just as when we hope to You and wait for Your help we are good to You, so may we be kind to You when our prayer has already been fulfilled... Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
"Many troubles have surrounded us, we called upon You, O Lord our God; You distanced [them] from us — we are in our iniquities."
When "many troubles surround us", when many troubles come upon us, "we call upon You, O Lord our God" — we call You, God; "You distanced from us" — once You have even [?] distanced the sufferings from us — "we are in our iniquities" — we are already back with our sins. Leket Amarim.
—o—
f) "Only the tree that you know is not a food tree, that you may destroy"
The rule for all prohibitions is that a doubt in Torah law is to be decided leniently; yet here, regarding a tree, it is said that even when there is a doubt whether the tree is a fruit tree, one may not cut it down until one is certain that it is not a fruit tree — for the life of a tree is, according to the Torah, as precious as the life of a person, and where life is in danger, with a human life, it is already "in doubt, be stringent"... Imrei Chen.
—o—
g) "And the officers shall speak further" (ibid., 20) [printed: "the judges"]
Rabbi Nachman of Bratslav was told that the Shpoler Zeide enumerates to every person who comes in to him all the sins he has committed.
To this Rabbi Nachman said:
In the verse it is told that the priest enumerated all those who need not go to war (see Rashi). But when it came to enumerating "the man who is fearful — fearful of the sins in his hands", the priests stopped enumerating, and this was done by the officers — because enumerating Jewish sins is something priests are not allowed to do..
—o—
A woman once came to the Seer of Lublin. The Seer began to enumerate which sins she had committed. Rabbi Naftali of Ropczyce was standing by and said:
"We do have a good God after all! He truly knows everything, and tells no one..."

A Groundless Reproach.
God-fearing and pious Rachel, who firmly believed that her young husband was as pious as she, found out that when he travels he behaves very freely and does not even pray. Wishing to see whether this was true, before his departure she packed the handkerchiefs into his tallis bag. In the first letter she received from him, he pointed out that she had forgotten to give him handkerchiefs. To this she replied at once:
— Dear Feivel, I put [?] the handkerchiefs in — pray to God and you will get them.

Little Letters from Zakopane.

[Humour and satire — "Der Kokh-Lefl"; humorous letter and a joke; Zakopane.]
From her to him.
My bright [?] cart-horse!
You are surely wondering why I haven't written for a whole week? That's because I am in litigation with an ordinary Zakopane man.
Well, you are after all my husband too, so I must tell you: listen to a story — last [?] Thursday I get up in the morning and want to wash, I take a look: in my jug there isn't a drop of water; I go in to my neighbour in the next room and ask him for a little water — and what does he do, the scoundrel (drań)? He gives me a kiss right on the neck! What do you say to such an outrage! Kissing a strange woman! And she not even powdered and manicured! Is that not a cheek! You think I'll let him off? He wanted me to make ... [?] of it, but I don't want to settle it any other way than amicably ("polubownie")... Strangers have intervened in this dispute and there is hope that we'll come to terms.
To the boarding house where I'm staying there came a great astronomer and physicist, a young man as good as gold, who gave a lecture on Einstein's theory. The lecturer showed that Einstein's theory does not recognise the present concepts of place, time and number.
Place: he explains that when a wife goes out, even though she declares that she is going shopping ("sprawunki"), it may well be that she is going to a friend ("przyjaciel") for a "heart-to-heart" talk.
Time: when the husband comes home while the wife is asleep and excuses himself to the... "old girl" [?] that it is only 1 o'clock at night, it may well be that it is already 6 in the morning.
Number: when at a party there are 4 men and 1 woman and they want to dance, they need not wait until three more girls arrive, but can start dancing at once and finally [?] come out "in pairs" ("do pary").
You see, dear Mendl, I understand everything, but the last one I can never grasp. Perhaps you know?
Your almost-faithful wife
Keyle Gnendl (Karola Benia).
